notes_list.title: Noun: Definition & Types
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A Noun is a word used as the name of a person, place, thing, animal, quality, idea or state.
• Major types: Proper, Common, Collective, Material and Abstract Noun.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: Rahul, Delhi, book, army, gold, honesty, childhood.

notes_list.title: Proper & Common Noun
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Proper Noun: Specific name of a person, place or thing.
• Common Noun: General name of a person, place, animal or thing.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: India → Proper Noun; country → Common Noun. Ram → Proper Noun; boy → Common Noun.

notes_list.title: Collective, Material & Abstract Noun
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Collective: Names a group — team, army, committee.
• Material: Names a substance — gold, silver, water.
• Abstract: Names a quality, state or idea — honesty, beauty, freedom.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Competitive exams frequently test identification and transformation of noun types.

notes_list.title: Pronoun: Definition & Types
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A Pronoun is a word used in place of a noun.
• Major types: Personal, Reflexive, Demonstrative, Relative, Interrogative, Indefinite and Distributive.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: I, we, you, he, she, it, they, myself, this, who, which, someone, each.

notes_list.title: Personal Pronoun
notes_list.basic_overview:
• First person: I, we
• Second person: you
• Third person: he, she, it, they
• Objective forms include me, us, him, her, them.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Pronoun case is important in error detection: between you and me, not between you and I.

notes_list.title: Relative Pronoun
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Relative pronouns connect a relative clause to a noun or pronoun.
• Common forms: who, whom, whose, which, that.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Who is generally used for persons as subject; whom is traditionally used as object; which for things; whose shows possession.

notes_list.title: Each, Every, Either, Neither
notes_list.basic_overview: • Each, every, either and neither generally take a singular noun and singular verb when used in their standard determiner/pronoun functions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: Each student is ready. Every boy has a book. Neither answer is correct. Either road leads to the town.

notes_list.title: Adjective: Definition & Types
notes_list.basic_overview:
• An Adjective qualifies or describes a noun or pronoun.
• Major types: Quality, Quantity, Number, Demonstrative, Possessive, Interrogative and Distributive.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: beautiful, honest, much, five, this, my, which, each.

notes_list.title: Degrees of Comparison
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Positive: tall
• Comparative: taller
• Superlative: tallest
• Irregular forms include good → better → best and bad → worse → worst.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Double comparatives such as 'more better' are incorrect.

notes_list.title: Verb: Definition & Types
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A Verb expresses an action, occurrence or state.
• Major classifications include Main Verb, Auxiliary Verb, Transitive Verb, Intransitive Verb, Modal Verb and Linking Verb.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: run, write, become, is, have, do, can, may, should.

notes_list.title: Transitive & Intransitive Verb
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Transitive Verb: takes an object.
• Intransitive Verb: does not require an object.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: She wrote a letter. → transitive. The baby slept. → intransitive.

notes_list.title: Finite & Non-Finite Verb
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Finite Verb: changes according to tense/person/number and forms the main predicate.
• Non-finite: infinitive, gerund and participle forms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: He goes. → finite. To go, going, gone → non-finite forms depending on usage.

notes_list.title: Adverb
notes_list.basic_overview:
• An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or sometimes an entire clause.
• Types include manner, place, time, frequency and degree.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: slowly, here, yesterday, always, very.

notes_list.title: Preposition
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A preposition shows relationship between a noun/pronoun and another word.
• Common forms: in, on, at, by, with, from, to, for, since, between, among.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Preposition-based error spotting is a common competitive-exam grammar area.

notes_list.title: Conjunction
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses.
• Coordinating: and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet.
• Subordinating: because, although, if, unless, while, since.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Correlative pairs include either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also.

notes_list.title: Interjection
notes_list.basic_overview:
• An interjection expresses sudden emotion or feeling.
• Examples: Hurrah!, Alas!, Wow!, Oh!, Bravo!
notes_list.extra_info_content: Interjections are generally followed by an exclamation mark when the sentence expresses strong emotion.

notes_list.title: Use of A and An
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A is generally used before a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound.
• An is generally used before a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Sound matters: a university, a European, an hour, an honest man.

notes_list.title: Use of The
notes_list.basic_overview: • 'The' is used with specific or previously identified nouns and with certain unique or conventional references.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common examples: the sun, the earth, the Ganges, the Himalayas, the United States.

notes_list.title: Zero Article
notes_list.basic_overview: • No article is often used with plural or uncountable nouns when speaking generally and with many proper names.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: Books are useful. Gold is precious. India is a country.

notes_list.title: Some, Any, Much, Many
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Many: countable plural nouns.
• Much: uncountable nouns.
• Some: commonly used in affirmative contexts.
• Any: commonly used in negatives and questions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: many books, much water, some money, any questions.

notes_list.title: Few, A Few, The Few
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Few: hardly any; negative sense.
• A few: some; positive sense.
• The few: the small number that exists.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Few students passed. A few students passed. The few students who passed were rewarded.

notes_list.title: Little, A Little, The Little
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used mainly with uncountable nouns.
• Little = almost none.
• A little = some.
• The little = the small amount available.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: There is little hope. There is a little hope. The little hope he had disappeared.

notes_list.title: Simple Present
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used for habits, routines, general truths, facts and repeated actions.
• Structure: Subject + V1/V1+s/es + Object.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The sun rises in the east. She goes to school every day.

notes_list.title: Present Continuous
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + is/am/are + V-ing.
• Used for an action happening around the present time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: They are studying now.

notes_list.title: Present Perfect
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + has/have + V3.
• Commonly expresses a completed action with present relevance or an experience.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: She has finished her work.

notes_list.title: Present Perfect Continuous
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + has/have been + V-ing.
• Used for an action continuing over a period up to the present.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He has been working for two hours.

notes_list.title: Simple Past
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + V2 + Object.
• Used for completed actions in the past.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: She visited Delhi last year.

notes_list.title: Past Continuous
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + was/were + V-ing.
• Used for an action in progress at a particular past time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: They were playing when it started raining.

notes_list.title: Past Perfect
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + had + V3.
• Commonly used for the earlier of two past actions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The train had left before we reached the station.

notes_list.title: Past Perfect Continuous
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + had been + V-ing.
• Used for an action continuing for a period before another past event.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He had been studying for three hours before dinner.

notes_list.title: Simple Future
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + will + V1.
• Used for future actions, decisions and predictions depending on context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: They will arrive tomorrow.

notes_list.title: Future Continuous
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + will be + V-ing.
• Used for an action that will be in progress at a future time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: I will be travelling tomorrow evening.

notes_list.title: Future Perfect
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Structure: Subject + will have + V3.
• Used for an action completed before a specified future time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: She will have completed the work by Monday.

notes_list.title: Singular Subject with Singular Verb
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A singular subject generally takes a singular verb in the simple present.
• Example: He works hard.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Be careful with intervening phrases: The quality of the apples is good.

notes_list.title: Each, Every, Either, Neither
notes_list.basic_overview: • Each, every, either and neither generally take singular verbs when they function as singular determiners/pronouns.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Each of the students is present. Neither of the answers is correct.

notes_list.title: Either...or / Neither...nor
notes_list.basic_overview: • With either...or and neither...nor, the verb generally agrees with the subject nearer to it in formal standard usage.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Neither the teacher nor the students are ready. Neither the students nor the teacher is ready.

notes_list.title: Collective Nouns & Agreement
notes_list.basic_overview: • Collective nouns can take singular or plural agreement depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individuals, especially in British usage.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The committee has decided. The committee are divided in their opinions.

notes_list.title: Active Voice: Concept
notes_list.basic_overview:
• In Active Voice, the subject performs the action.
• Example: Ram writes a letter.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Structure generally follows Subject + Verb + Object.

notes_list.title: Passive Voice: Concept
notes_list.basic_overview:
• In Passive Voice, the receiver of the action becomes the grammatical subject.
• Example: A letter is written by Ram.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Core pattern: Object + suitable form of be + V3 + optional by + agent.

notes_list.title: Voice Change: Tense Rules
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Present Simple → am/is/are + V3
• Past Simple → was/were + V3
• Present Continuous → am/is/are being + V3
• Past Continuous → was/were being + V3
• Present Perfect → has/have been + V3
• Past Perfect → had been + V3
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 The object of an active transitive sentence generally becomes the subject of the passive sentence.

notes_list.title: Modal Passive
notes_list.basic_overview: • Modal + V1 in active commonly becomes modal + be + V3 in passive.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: You must obey the rules. → The rules must be obeyed.

notes_list.title: Direct Speech
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Direct speech reports the speaker's exact words within quotation marks.
• Example: He said, "I am tired."
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Quotation marks are used to show the exact words of the speaker.

notes_list.title: Indirect Speech
notes_list.basic_overview: • Indirect speech reports the meaning of the speaker's words without quoting the exact wording.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He said that he was tired.

notes_list.title: Backshift of Tense
notes_list.basic_overview:
• When the reporting verb is in the past, tense backshift commonly occurs where appropriate.
• Present → Past; Past → Past Perfect in many contexts.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He said, "I work hard." → He said that he worked hard.

notes_list.title: Pronoun & Time-Expression Changes
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Pronouns change according to speaker/listener/reference.
• Time expressions may change: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the previous day.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Changes depend on context; they are not mechanical in every sentence.

notes_list.title: Imperative, Interrogative & Exclamatory Sentences
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Imperative sentences commonly use reporting verbs such as ordered, requested, advised, told depending on meaning.
• Questions use asked/enquired.
• Exclamations use suitable reporting verbs such as exclaimed with joy/sorrow.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He said to me, "Please help me." → He requested me to help him.

notes_list.title: Can & Could
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Can expresses ability, possibility or permission depending on context.
• Could can express past ability, polite requests or possibility.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: She can swim. Could you help me? He could run fast when he was young.

notes_list.title: May & Might
notes_list.basic_overview:
• May commonly expresses possibility or permission.
• Might generally expresses a more tentative possibility.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: It may rain. He might come later.

notes_list.title: Must & Should
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Must commonly expresses strong obligation or necessity.
• Should commonly expresses advice, expectation or mild obligation.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: You must follow the rules. You should revise regularly.

notes_list.title: Need & Dare
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Need and dare can function as ordinary verbs or, in certain constructions, as marginal modals.
• Competitive exams frequently test their negative/question forms.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Need I go? / You need not worry. Usage depends on grammatical construction.

notes_list.title: To-Infinitive
notes_list.basic_overview:
• The basic infinitive is generally to + V1.
• Example: to read, to write, to study.
notes_list.extra_info_content: After certain modal verbs, bare infinitive is used: can go, should study, must work.

notes_list.title: Bare Infinitive
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Bare infinitive means V1 without 'to'.
• It occurs after modal auxiliaries and in certain causative/perception constructions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: She can swim. I made him work. I saw him cross the road.

notes_list.title: Gerund: Verb + ing as Noun
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A gerund is an -ing form functioning as a noun.
• Example: Swimming is good exercise.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common verbs followed by gerund include enjoy, avoid, admit, deny, suggest and finish.

notes_list.title: Present & Past Participle
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Present participle generally ends in -ing.
• Past participle is commonly V3.
• Participles can function adjectivally or form verb phrases.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: a crying baby, a broken chair, the written answer.

notes_list.title: In, On, At
notes_list.basic_overview:
• At: specific time — at 5 o'clock.
• On: days/dates — on Monday, on 15 August.
• In: months, years, seasons and longer periods — in March, in 2026.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 'At night' is a common fixed expression.

notes_list.title: Since & For
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Since: starting point of time.
• For: duration of time.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: since Monday, since 2020, for two hours, for five years.

notes_list.title: In, On, At for Place
notes_list.basic_overview:
• In indicates enclosure or area.
• On indicates surface.
• At commonly indicates a point or location.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: in the room, on the table, at the station.

notes_list.title: Between & Among
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Between is traditionally used for distinct individual relationships, often two but not necessarily limited to two.
• Among is commonly used for a group or undifferentiated mass.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: between A and B; among friends.

notes_list.title: FANBOYS
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Coordinating conjunctions include for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
• They connect elements of equal grammatical status.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Memory aid: FANBOYS = For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.

notes_list.title: Either...or / Neither...nor
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Correlative conjunctions work in pairs.
• Common pairs: either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Parallel structure is important: She likes both reading and writing.

notes_list.title: Assertive, Interrogative, Imperative & Exclamatory
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Assertive — statement.
• Interrogative — question.
• Imperative — command, request, advice or instruction.
• Exclamatory — strong emotion.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: He is honest. / Is he honest? / Be honest. / How honest he is!

notes_list.title: Simple Sentence
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A simple sentence contains one independent clause.
• It may contain multiple phrases and a compound subject or object.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The boy worked hard.

notes_list.title: Compound Sentence
notes_list.basic_overview: • A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses generally joined by coordinating conjunctions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He worked hard, and he succeeded.

notes_list.title: Complex Sentence
notes_list.basic_overview: • A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Although he was tired, he continued working.

notes_list.title: Affirmative to Negative
notes_list.basic_overview: • Sentence meaning should remain unchanged while converting affirmative and negative forms where the question requires equivalent meaning.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: Everyone likes him. → There is no one who does not like him.

notes_list.title: Basic Question Tag Rule
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A positive statement generally takes a negative tag.
• A negative statement generally takes a positive tag.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He is honest, isn't he? / He isn't honest, is he?

notes_list.title: Special Cases
notes_list.basic_overview:
• I am → aren't I? is a common standard form.
• Imperatives commonly take will you/won't you/can you depending on meaning.
• Let's → shall we?
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: I am late, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Open the door, will you?

notes_list.title: Zero Conditional
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used for general truths and facts.
• Structure: If + Present Simple, Present Simple.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: If you heat ice, it melts.

notes_list.title: First Conditional
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used for real or possible future conditions.
• If + Present Simple, will + V1.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: If it rains, we will stay home.

notes_list.title: Second Conditional
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used for hypothetical or unlikely present/future situations.
• If + Past Simple, would + V1.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: If I had more time, I would travel.

notes_list.title: Third Conditional
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Used for unreal situations in the past.
• If + Past Perfect, would have + V3.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: If he had studied, he would have passed.

notes_list.title: Positive, Comparative & Superlative
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Positive: no comparison — tall.
• Comparative: comparison between two — taller.
• Superlative: comparison among three or more — tallest.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Common irregular forms: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst; little → less → least; much/many → more → most.

notes_list.title: Subject-Verb Error
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Incorrect: He go to school.
• Correct: He goes to school.
• Always check subject-verb agreement.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Error-detection questions frequently test number agreement, especially with long subjects and intervening phrases.

notes_list.title: Article Error
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Incorrect article usage is a common source of grammar errors.
• Article selection depends on sound, specificity and noun type.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: He is an honest man. Not: He is a honest man.

notes_list.title: Preposition Error
notes_list.basic_overview: • Common exam errors involve incorrect combinations such as discuss about, order for, enter into in certain standard constructions.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: We discussed the issue. 'Discuss about the issue' is generally treated as incorrect in standard exam grammar.

notes_list.title: Pronoun Error
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Check pronoun case, antecedent agreement, person and number.
• Example: Each student must bring his or her ID in formal traditional exam grammar.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Modern English increasingly uses singular 'they' in many contexts, but exam questions may follow the convention specified by the test.

notes_list.title: Common Competitive-Exam Synonyms
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Abandon — Leave, Forsake
• Abundant — Plentiful, Ample
• Accurate — Correct, Precise
• Brave — Courageous, Bold
• Candid — Frank, Honest
• Diligent — Industrious, Hard-working
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Synonym questions test contextual similarity, not always exact equivalence.

notes_list.title: Common Competitive-Exam Antonyms
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Ancient — Modern
• Artificial — Natural
• Expand — Contract
• Generous — Stingy
• Humble — Arrogant
• Permanent — Temporary
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📚 Antonym selection depends on the exact meaning of the given word in context.

notes_list.title: Important One Word Substitutions
notes_list.basic_overview:
• One who loves mankind — Philanthropist
• One who hates mankind — Misanthrope
• One who knows many languages — Polyglot
• One who cannot read or write — Illiterate
• One who speaks two languages — Bilingual
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 One-word substitution is frequently tested through direct definition-to-word questions.

notes_list.title: Important Idioms
notes_list.basic_overview:
• A blessing in disguise — something that seems bad but has a good result.
• Break the ice — start a conversation or reduce tension.
• Once in a blue moon — very rarely.
• Hit the nail on the head — describe something exactly.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Idiom questions usually ask for meaning, suitable usage or replacement.

notes_list.title: Accept & Except
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Accept: receive or agree to.
• Except: excluding.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: I accept your proposal. Everyone came except Ravi.

notes_list.title: Affect & Effect
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Affect: commonly used as a verb meaning influence.
• Effect: commonly used as a noun meaning result.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The weather affected the match. The effect was significant.

notes_list.title: Principal & Principle
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Principal: chief/head or a sum of money.
• Principle: fundamental rule or belief.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Example: The principal addressed the students. Honesty is an important principle.

notes_list.title: Stationary & Stationery
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Stationary: not moving.
• Stationery: writing materials.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Memory aid: stationery with 'e' → envelopes and writing equipment.

notes_list.title: Full Stop, Comma & Semicolon
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Full stop ends a declarative sentence.
• Comma separates elements and clauses in various constructions.
• Semicolon can connect closely related independent clauses.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Punctuation questions may test comma placement, apostrophe and sentence boundaries.

notes_list.title: Apostrophe & Quotation Marks
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Apostrophe indicates possession or contractions.
• Quotation marks indicate direct speech or quoted material.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Examples: Rahul's book. Don't go. He said, "I am ready."

notes_list.title: Error Detection Checklist
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Check Subject-Verb Agreement.
• Check Tense.
• Check Articles and Determiners.
• Check Prepositions.
• Check Pronouns.
• Check Conjunctions.
• Check Adjective/Adverb usage.
• Check Parallelism and Redundancy.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Suggested checking order: Verb → Subject → Tense → Pronoun → Article → Preposition → Conjunction → Modifier → Idiomatic usage.

notes_list.title: Cloze Test Approach
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Identify the grammatical role required by the blank.
• Check tense, subject-verb agreement, article, preposition, conjunction and vocabulary.
• Read the complete sentence and paragraph before final selection.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Context is essential: two grammatically possible options may differ in meaning or collocation.

notes_list.title: Sentence Improvement Rules
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Identify the underlined/error segment.
• Check grammar first, then idiomatic usage and meaning.
• Avoid changing a grammatically correct sentence merely because another form sounds different.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 🎯 Important areas: tense, articles, prepositions, subject-verb agreement, comparison, modifiers and parallelism.

notes_list.title: Grammar-Based Fillers
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Determine whether the blank requires a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction or determiner.
• Check grammatical agreement and context.
notes_list.extra_info_content: 📌 Collocations and fixed expressions are especially important in vocabulary-based fillers.

notes_list.title: Sentence Arrangement Logic
notes_list.basic_overview:
• Identify the opening sentence using introductory context.
• Find mandatory pairs through pronouns, connectors and logical references.
• Track chronology, cause-effect and conclusion markers.
notes_list.extra_info_content: Useful connectors: however, therefore, moreover, consequently, first, finally, this, these, such, hence.
